items.text: In Finland, blueberries are more than a healthy snack; they are part of the national culture. Thanks to the so-called everyman’s right, people can freely enter forests and collect berries if they don’t disturb others. Each summer, families head out together, and knowledge about the best blueberry spots often passes from one generation to the next. Blogger Varpu Rusila explains that picking blueberries is both a tradition and a way to appreciate nature. Blueberries appear everywhere in Finnish life. They are in breakfast porridge, smoothies, ice cream, and the famous mustikkapiirakka, or blueberry pie. Families prepare simple recipes at home, often using wild blueberries because they are smaller, tastier, and richer in nutrients than farmed ones. Blueberries are also part of daily life in Helsinki, where people enjoy blueberry products in markets, cafés, and restaurants. The fruit is seen as both food and a cultural symbol. For Finns, blueberry picking connects health, family, and their close relationship with forests. Difficult words: spot (a place or location), appreciate (to be thankful for something or to see its value), nutrient (a substance that helps the body grow and stay healthy). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

In Finland, blueberries are not only food but also an important part of life. People can go into forests and pick berries freely . Families go together each summer, and children learn the best places from their parents. Blogger Varpu Rusila says blueberry picking is a way to enjoy nature. Blueberries are in many dishes. People use them in porridge , smoothies, ice cream, and blueberry pie. Finns usually choose wild blueberries because they are small, dark, and full of taste and vitamins. In Helsinki, blueberries are everywhere. Shops, cafés, and markets sell products with blueberries. For Finns, blueberries give both health and happiness, and they show the strong connection between people and nature. Difficult words: freely (without limit), porridge (soft food made by cooking oats in water or milk), connection (a link between two things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Blueberries are very special in Finland. People love them. In summer, many people go to the forest to pick them. They can do it freely . Families go together. Children learn from their parents where to pick blueberries. Blogger Varpu Rusila says that picking blueberries is fun and a way to love nature . Finnish people eat blueberries every day. They put them in porridge , pie, ice cream, and smoothies. Wild blueberries are small and very tasty. They also help people stay strong and healthy. In Helsinki, people see blueberries in many places. Shops and cafés sell food with blueberries. For Finnish people, blueberries mean health, family time, and love for the forest. Difficult words: freely (without limit or rule), nature (the world of trees, animals, land, and so on), porridge (soft food when you cook oats in water or milk). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Saunas have been part of human culture for thousands of years, from Finnish sauna traditions to Japanese onsen and Indigenous sweat lodges. Modern science is now studying their effects on health. A long-term Finnish study of over 2,000 men found that frequent sauna use was linked to better heart health, lower blood pressure, healthier cholesterol, and reduced risk of death. Saunas reach up to 90°C with low humidity, triggering the body’s thermoregulatory system: blood vessels widen, heart rate rises, skin absorbs heat, and sweating cools the body. This reaction is similar to moderate exercise, which may strengthen the cardiovascular system. Sauna use may also aid muscle recovery after workouts by improving blood flow, reducing excess inflammation , and helping the body clear waste. Another benefit is the production of heat shock proteins, which repair DNA and support cell health. However, scientists caution that research is still limited to certain groups and lifestyles, and high heat may be unsafe for some people, such as those with health conditions. Difficult words: thermoregulatory (controlling body temperature), cardiovascular (related to the heart and blood vessels), inflammation (the body’s natural reaction to injury or infection, often causing pain or swelling). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

People started using saunas and hot baths thousands of years ago, but scientists are only now learning how they affect health. A Finnish study of more than 2,000 men showed that those who used saunas often were healthier, with lower blood pressure, better cholesterol, and less risk of dying early. In a sauna, the heat up to 90°C makes your heart beat faster, your blood vessels open, and your body sweat . This looks like exercise, and it may make the heart stronger. Saunas may also help muscles recover after sports by improving blood flow and reducing inflammation . Heat can also increase special proteins that repair cells. Still, scientists say saunas are not safe for everyone, and there needs to be more research to know all the benefits and limits. Difficult words: vessel (a tube in your body through which blood travels), sweat (when your skin gets wet after an exercise or when you are hot), inflammation (the body’s reaction to injury or infection). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Saunas are hot rooms which people use for health and relaxation . They are old traditions in many countries, like Finland and Japan. Scientists study 2,000 Finnish men. They find that people who go to saunas often are healthier. They have lower blood pressure , better heart health, and live longer. In a sauna, the heat up to 90°C makes you sweat , your heart beat faster, and your blood move quickly. This is like doing exercise. Saunas may also help tired muscles after sport and make the body stronger. Heat can also help repair cells in the body. But saunas are not safe for everyone, for example, pregnant women or those with health problems. Difficult words: relaxation (when you rest and feel calm), blood pressure (the power your blood goes through your body), sweat (when your skin gets wet after an exercise or when you are hot). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A court in New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay a huge fine of 567 million dollars for failing to protect children on its platforms, including Facebook and Instagram. The judge called Meta a public nuisance , and explained that the company knowingly allowed child safety risks and sexual exploitation to harm young users and their families. This new ruling brings Meta’s total fines in this major legal case to almost one billion dollars. In addition to paying money, Meta must change several policies, such as stopping children from using AI chatbots for adult conversations. Meta disagrees with the decision, claims it works hard to keep teenagers safe, and plans to appeal. Experts compare this legal situation to past cases against big tobacco companies, and they expect that economic penalties will finally force tech companies to prioritize safety over profits. Meanwhile, experts continue to debate whether strict government regulations or parental guidance is the best way to protect young internet users today. Difficult words: nuisance (something that causes harm, trouble, or danger), exploitation (using someone unfairly or harmfully for your own advantage or financial gain), prioritize (to put something first because it is the most important thing). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A court in New Mexico gave Meta a big fine of 567 million dollars. The judge said Meta didn’t keep children safe on Facebook and Instagram. The court found that Meta knew about dangerous online harms but didn’t stop them. Now, Meta must pay almost one billion dollars in total from this court case. Part of this money will help young people who were hurt by social media. Meta must also change its rules to protect children from dangerous AI chat tools. Meta says it works hard to keep teenagers safe and will try to change the judge’s decision. Some people believe that big fines are necessary to force tech companies to protect children. Others think that parents and young people should learn to use the internet safely together instead of making strict new laws. Difficult words: fine (money a person or company must pay for breaking a rule or law), in total (including everything or everyone when added together), force (to make someone do something they might not want to do). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A court in the US tells Meta to pay a very big fine . Meta owns Facebook and Instagram. The judge says Meta does not protect children on the internet. The company knows about online dangers, but it does not help young people. Now Meta must pay lots of money to help children who are hurt. Meta must also make new rules for its apps. Meta says it tries to keep young people safe. The company wants to fight the court decision . Some people want more rules to stop bad things online. Other people think that children need better help from their parents to stay safe online. Difficult words: fine (money a person or company must pay for breaking a rule), protect (to keep someone safe), decision (what you want to do after thinking). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In many European countries, families are facing growing school expenses, which often rise faster than inflation. The largest costs usually come from textbooks, which in Spain and Italy can represent over 70% of the total. In Italy, consumer groups complain that families must often buy new editions instead of second-hand books, creating unnecessary costs. Spanish families pay around 500 euros yearly, most of it for books. Germany faces some of the highest costs, with families spending about 3,600 euros per year, well above inflation. School trips, reaching 2,000 euros annually, are the main burden , although some states limit spending. In the UK, costs grew by 30% in just two years, mostly because of food. Meals and snacks for one secondary pupil can exceed 900 euros a year, while uniforms remain expensive for families with more children. France is the exception. Families there spend only around 211 euros yearly, thanks to a recycling system for textbooks and a government allowance of 450 euros per pupil, which reduces the overall pressure. Difficult words: burden (a heavy problem or responsibility), allowance (money given regularly to help with costs). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Families in Europe pay more and more for school, and in many countries the costs grow faster than inflation . Textbooks are usually the most expensive part. In Spain, books account for more than 70% of the total, and in Italy, parents must buy new editions , which makes the situation harder. German families face very high prices, around 3,600 euros a year, with school trips costing about 2,000 euros. In the UK, costs are over 2,600 euros, and they grew by 30% in two years. Meals and snacks are the biggest part of the increase, while uniforms are still expensive. France is different. Families there spend only 211 euros a year. This is because children get free textbooks, and the state pays an extra 450 euros for every pupil . Difficult words: inflation (rise in prices), edition (a version of a book), pupil (a young student). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

School is very expensive in many European countries. Prices go up every year. Parents pay the most money for textbooks . In Spain, books are more than half of the costs . In Italy, families buy new editions and pay even more. In Germany, school is very expensive. One child can cost 3,600 euros every year. School trips are the biggest part. In the UK, parents spend more than 2,600 euros. Food is very expensive. Snacks and meals take a lot of money, and uniforms are not cheap. In France, school is not so expensive. Parents pay about 211 euros a year. Children get free textbooks, and every family gets 450 euros from the state. This helps many families. Difficult words: textbook (a school book), costs (how much money you need to buy or do something), edition (a new version of a book). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The EU has introduced the new Entry/Exit System (EES) for non-EU travelers entering the Schengen area. This digital system replaces manual passport stamps with biometric checks, including facial images and fingerprint scanning. Travelers first register at self-service kiosks and then meet a border officer for verification. While a regular passport check takes about 60 seconds, this new process takes around 90 seconds. These extra seconds quickly cause severe congestion when thousands of passengers pass through busy airports every day. Long queues stretching hundreds of meters have caused travelers to wait up to five hours, which leads to missed flights. Different hardware and software across EU member states make it more difficult to fix technical problems. Additionally, travelers cannot complete any steps in advance before arriving. Greece received a temporary exemption to use ordinary passport checks, and airport leaders are calling for full suspensions during peak travel times. Authorities hope to add more self-service kiosks by fall to reduce long airport lines. Difficult words: biometric (using unique physical characteristics of a person such as face shape or fingerprints to prove who they are), congestion (a situation where a place is crowded and full of traffic or people), exemption (special permission to not follow a rule that other people or places must follow). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The EU introduced a new digital entry system for travelers coming from non-EU countries. The system uses face scans and fingerprints instead of regular paper passport stamps. Travelers must first scan their passports at a special kiosk machine and then talk to a border officer. The new process takes longer than before. It adds thirty extra seconds for every person. Because thousands of people travel every day, very long lines are forming at major European airports. Some people have to wait up to five hours and even miss their airplanes. The situation is difficult because different countries use different software, and travelers cannot prepare online before they arrive at airport controls. Greece is currently allowed to keep old passport checks. Airport leaders want to pause the new system during the busy summer season to help travelers. Difficult words: fingerprint (the mark your finger leaves on things), kiosk machine (a small, self-service computer screen in a public place), major (very large or important). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The European Union has a new digital passport system. It uses photos of faces and fingerprints for people from non-EU countries. Travelers go to a machine first. Then they see a border officer. The new check takes extra time for every person. Now, airports in Europe have very long lines. Some travelers wait for many hours. They miss their planes. Different airports use different machines, so it is hard to solve problems. Today, travelers cannot do any checks on their phones before they travel. Greece can still use old passport stamps. Airport leaders want to stop the new system during the summer months to help people travel fast. Difficult words: passport (an official document which you need to travel to other countries), fingerprint (the mark your finger leaves on things), miss (to arrive too late to catch a bus, train, or plane). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Millions of pieces of space debris now orbit Earth, ranging from tiny particles to large objects like old satellites or even a car. These fragments move extremely fast and threaten working satellites that support our modern technologies. Collisions in space can create thousands of new fragments, increasing the danger of a chain reaction known as the Kessler syndrome. Although most debris burns when re-entering Earth’s atmosphere, large pieces can sometimes survive and fall to the ground. Scientists are testing ways to solve this growing problem. Some ideas include cleaning old junk using lasers or space tug boats that move debris to safer orbits. Others focus on repairing or refueling satellites so they don’t turn into junk. Reducing new waste, controlling satellite re-entry, and improving international rules are key to keeping space safe for the future. Difficult words: fragment (a small part of a larger object), tug (a small, strong vehicle that pulls or moves bigger objects), refuel (to put more fuel into something, like a rocket or satellite, so it can keep working). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

There is a lot of trash flying around the Earth. It comes from old satellites , rockets, and other broken things. This trash, called space junk, moves very fast and can hit working satellites. When satellites crash, they make even more trash. Some of it burns when it falls back to Earth, but big pieces can sometimes reach the ground. Scientists and companies are looking for ways to fix this problem. They want to stop making new trash and clean up the old one. Some use special satellites or lasers to move the junk. They also want to make sure old satellites fall safely. We must keep the space clean if we want to keep using it. Difficult words: trash (waste or things that people don’t want to use anymore), satellite (a machine that goes around Earth), laser (a strong beam of light). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

There is a lot of trash around the Earth. It comes from old rockets and satellites . The trash moves very fast. It can hit other satellites. Then there is more trash. Some trash falls and burns in the air. Big pieces can come to Earth. Scientists want to clean space. They try to use lasers or new machines to move the trash. They also want to stop making more trash. People must take care of space. It is important for phones, the internet, and TV. We need to keep it safe and clean. Difficult words: satellite (a machine which goes around the Earth), hit (to crash into something), laser (a strong light beam). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A shocking video from Ukraine shows a Russian drone chasing a street vegetable seller named Yuri in Kherson. Although the drone exploded nearby and injured him, Yuri miraculously survived. Ukrainians call these disturbing civilian attacks a human safari, where Russian operators use drones to target ordinary citizens instead of military forces. Drones have completely transformed the modern battlefield. Russian troops employ various models, including fast kamikaze drones , commercial quadcopters , and advanced fiber-optic drones that cannot be easily jammed by radio signals. Both Ukraine and Russia have established specialized military branches dedicated to drone warfare where technology evolves every few weeks. Beyond drone attacks, Russia continues to strike Ukrainian cities with deadly ballistic missiles. Recent missile strikes killed at least twenty-one people and hit a rural railway station and surrounding warehouses. Ukrainian air defenses are struggling because they are running out of critical interceptor missiles, which leaves civilians vulnerable to continued destruction across the country. Difficult words: disturbing (something that makes you feel worried, sad, or uncomfortable), kamikaze drone (a small flying machine packed with explosives that flies directly into a target and destroys itself when it hits), quadcopter (a small aircraft or drone that flies using four spinning blades). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A dangerous video shows a Russian drone chasing a street seller named Yuri in southern Ukraine. The drone exploded, but Yuri survived with injuries. People call these attacks on regular citizens a human safari. Drones are now very important in this war. Russian soldiers use different types of drones to attack people and military locations. Some drones travel very fast, while others use long cables so their signals cannot be blocked. Technology changes quickly, and both armies now have special drone teams. At the same time, heavy attacks continue to destroy buildings and harm people. A recent attack on a train station killed eight citizens. Ukraine needs more missiles to stop these dangerous air attacks, but its supplies are running low. Because of this, many people remain in danger every day. Difficult words: chase (to run or fly quickly after someone or something to try to catch them), citizen (a regular person who belongs to a country and is not in the military), supply (an amount of something you keep ready to be used). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

There is a video of a Russian drone. The drone is following a man in Ukraine. The man sells vegetables on the street. The drone explodes near him, but he lives. Russian soldiers use many small drones to attack people and cars in cities. Drones are now very important in the war. Some drones fly very fast. Some drones use long wires . These drones are hard to track . Today, both Ukraine and Russia have special teams for drones. Russia also uses big rockets to attack towns. One rocket hits a train station and kills eight people. Ukraine needs more help and more air defense to stop these bad attacks and save lives. Difficult words: important (when something matters or has a big impact), wire (a long, thin piece of metal), track (to follow something or someone over time), air defense (rockets which shoot down other rockets or drones in the sky). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Lake Gatun was flooded in 1913 to create the Panama Canal that connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. This canal serves as a crucial global commerce transit route. However, due to climate change exacerbating El Niño, one of the driest years on record for the Panama Canal has occurred. This leads to an unusual sight of trees protruding from the water during the rainy season when the lake should be at its highest. This low water level is limiting vessel passage, affecting global trade. Some ships face longer routes around South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope or the Suez Canal, while others engage in bidding wars for canal slots , which results in increased shipping time and costs. The issue is anticipated to worsen as Central America is expected to receive less rainfall in the future due to climate change. Fixing the problem could cost billions and take years if it’s even possible. Difficult words: exacerbate (to make a problem or bad situation more intense), protrude (to stick out), slot (a place in an arrangement or scheme). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

In 1913, workers flooded Lake Gatun to make the Panama Canal. The canal became an important link between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans for global business. But climate change, and especially El Niño, brought one of the driest years recorded for the canal during the rainy season. It is even possible to see trees sticking out from the water. The low water levels mean problems for big ships which want to pass through and this has an impact on global trade . Some ships now have to travel around the Cape of Good Hope or the Suez Canal. Others bid for canal access, which causes delays and higher shipping costs. It seems that the situation will get even worse in the future because there will probably be even less rain in the area. It is not clear how to solve this problem and if it is even possible because it would cost very much money. Difficult words: link (something what connects two things), global trade (when countries do business with each other), bid (to offer a certain price for something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Panama Canal connects two oceans, the Atlantic and the Pacific Ocean. In 1913, workers must flood Lake Gatun to make the canal. The canal is very important for global trade . Big ships go through the canal. The canal makes the way much shorter. But there is a problem – not enough rain. This year, the canal has very low water. You can even see trees in the water. It is not usual. This makes it hard for ships to pass. They have to go around Africa or Egypt. It takes more time and money. This problem will get worse because Central America will have even less rain in the future. Experts do not know how to solve it or if it is even possible. Difficult words: canal (a long thin stretch of water for boats and ships to travel along), flood (to cover with water), global trade (when countries do business together). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Pop icon Madonna gave Vogue an exclusive tour of her London home to share the story behind some of her most cherished personal possessions. She started in her office by showing a self-portrait by Frida Kahlo. When she saw a postcard of the painting during her first minutes in New York inspired her to eventually buy it at an auction 11 years later. Madonna also highlighted special family mementos , including a wooden rosary that belonged to her late mother, post-it notes from her daughter, and a unique sculpture gifted by her son Rocco. In her living room, she revealed a second Frida Kahlo piece depicting birth, which deeply connects to her experience of growing up motherless. Finally, in her bedroom, Madonna showed first-edition books, a blanket crocheted by her daughter during quarantine, and a plush octopus named Octavia – a meaningful gift from her sister that reminds her of a dedicated nurse who supported her through a serious hospital stay. Difficult words: cherished (loved very much and protected because it is extremely special to you), memento (a small object that you keep to remember a person, place, or event), rosary (a string of small beads used by religious people while saying prayers). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Madonna invited Vogue into her home in London to show her favorite personal objects. She began with a self-portrait by Mexican painter Frida Kahlo, which she dreamed of owning when she first moved to New York. She also shared sentimental family items, such as her mother’s wooden rosary , a sculpture made by her son Rocco, and a soft blanket crocheted by her daughter Esther. In her living room, she showed another powerful painting by Frida Kahlo about mother-child connections. Finally, in her bedroom, Madonna showed two special first-edition books and a plush octopus named Octavia. She explained that the octopus helps her remember a kind nurse who looked after her while she was very sick in the hospital. Difficult words: sentimental (connected to warm personal memories and feelings rather than how much money something costs), rosary (a string of beads which people use shen they speak to a god), crochet (to make woolen clothes with a special hooked needle). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Famous singer Madonna shows Vogue her house in London. She has many special things there. She loves them. First, she shows a famous painting by Frida Kahlo. She buys it after moving to New York. She also shows things from her family, like her mother’s wooden rosary and a sculpture by her son. Her daughter makes her a warm blanket during COVID quarantine. In her bedroom, Madonna showsher favorite books and a toy octopus named Octavia. A nurse helps Madonna in the hospital. The toy makes her think of that nurse. Difficult words: rosary (beads which people use shen they speak to a god), blanket (a soft cover which keeps you warm), nurse (a person who takes care of people in hospital). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Professor Scot Lear points out that around 80% of New Year’s resolutions fail. He attributes this to the prevalence of vague goals like exercising more or eating better. To address this, he introduces the SMART acronym , emphasizing goals that are Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Timely. SMART goals are clear and achievable, like exercising three times a week for 30 minutes for three months. He emphasizes that setbacks are natural but encourages focusing on progress and learning. Self-compassion is essential, too, since progress isn’t always linear . In conclusion, Lear suggests being kinder to oneself, understanding that mistakes happen, and the key is to keep trying. Difficult words: acronym (a word formed from the initial letters of other words), setback (a problem or difficulty in progress), linear (progressing directly and predictably). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Professor Scot Lear reveals that approximately 80% of New Year’s resolutions fail. He believes that the rate is so high because people set vague goals, such as exercising more or eating better. To improve the chances of success, he introduces the SMART acronym . The goals should be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Timely. For example, a SMART goal could be exercising three times a week for 30 minutes over three months. Lear says that setbacks are normal and he emphasizes that it is important to stay focused on progress . We need to be kind to ourselves and understand that progress is not always straightforward. Difficult words: New Year’s resolution (when we decide to change something in our life and start doing it on 1 January), acronym (a word which we make from the first letters of other words), progress (when we get better at something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A New Year’s resolution is a promise which you make to yourself. You say that you will start doing something good or stop doing something bad on 1 January. Many people have problems with New Year’s resolutions. They often fail. Professor Scot Lear says that our goals must be SMART – Specific , Measurable , Achievable , Relevant , and Timely. An example is exercising three times a week for 30 minutes for three months. If there are problems, it is okay. Things are not always as we want. Scot says that we must be kind to ourselves, learn from our mistakes, and not stop. Difficult words: specific (clear), measurable (possible to measure), achievable (possible to do), relevant (useful, related to you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A new study has revealed European children and adolescents are in worse physical shape today than at almost any point over the last 60 years. Researchers from the University of Zaragoza analyzed physical fitness data from over 417,000 young people aged 6 to 16 across 20 European countries. The findings show a worrying long-term decline in key health indicators , including muscular strength, flexibility, and overall body composition . Upper and lower body strength have steadily dropped since the 1980s, while flexibility has experienced the steepest decline, and accelerated sharply after 2000. Additionally, researchers noted a continuous increase in body fat levels among youth. Health experts warn that physical inactivity severely threatens future well-being, as over 75% of European adolescents fail to meet the WHO’s recommendation of 60 minutes of daily physical activity. Difficult words: indicator (a sign or measurement that shows the condition or state of something), composition (the balance of fat and muscle in a body), accelerate (to start moving faster or to happen more quickly than before). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A new study shows that young people in Europe are in much worse physical shape today than in past decades . Researchers looked at health data for more than 417,000 children and teenagers from 20 European countries. They found that overall muscle strength and flexibility dropped dramatically over the last forty years. Especially after the year 2000, children became much less flexible . At the same time, body fat levels continue to grow. Health experts explain that good physical health in childhood helps prevent serious diseases like heart problems and diabetes later in life. But more than 75% of European teenagers don’t exercise for 60 minutes every day as recommended by the World Health Organization. Experts warn that public groups must quickly encourage young people to move more. Difficult words: decade (a period of 10 years), flxible (able to bend easily without breaking), encourage (to give someone support, confidence, or hope to do something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A big new study shows that children in Europe are not as strong as before. Experts check the health of over 417,000 children in 20 countries. They find that young people have less muscle strength and less flexibility than children forty years ago. Many children also have more body fat now. Doctors say that playing and exercising helps keep hearts and bodies healthy for the future. But more than 75% of teenagers in Europe do not move enough every day. Experts say that schools and cities must help children exercise more every day. It is the best way to stay healthy. Difficult words: health (how your body and mind feel), muscle strength (how much you can push, pull, or lift), flexibility (when you can stretch and move your body easily). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Perth Mint in Western Australia has set a new Guinness World Record by creating the world’s largest gold bar that weighs a massive 521.2 kilograms. Crafted from Australian gold, the bar achieved a purity level of 99.999 percent, and exceeded the standard 99.99 percent global purity benchmark . Chief executive Paul Graham called the project a miracle, and said that more than 35 specialists worked on the three-day creation while official Guinness judges monitored every step. The huge bar shatters the previous 300-kilogram record set in Dubai two years ago. While its metal value alone exceeds 100 million dollars, its true worth lies in showing Australia’s advanced refining skills to global markets. The record-breaking bar, nicknamed the People’s Bar, will soon go on display alongside the Mint’s famous one-tonne gold coin. This achievement highlights Australia’s booming gold sector, with export earnings predicted to reach 60 billion dollars as gold rises to become the nation’s second-largest export. Difficult words: purity (how clean or natural something is, without any other metals or bad materials mixed in), bebchmark (a standard or model that other things are measured or compared against), shatter (to break or surpass a previous record by a very large amount), refine (to make a substance pure by removing unwanted materials from it). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The Perth Mint in Australia made the world’s biggest gold bar which weighs 521.2 kilograms. It broke the old record of 300 kilograms held by Dubai. Over 35 experts worked together for three days to make it, and judges from Guinness World Records watched the whole process. The bar is special because it has a very high purity of 99.999 percent, which is extremely difficult to achieve . The metal alone is worth more than 100 million dollars, but the bar was created to show the world how skilled Australian gold makers are. People will soon be able to see the giant bar on display at the Perth Mint. Today, gold is a very important business in Australia. It brings in billions of dollars in exports every year. Difficult words: purity (how clean or natural something is, without any other metals or bad materials mixed in), achieve (to successfully reach a goal or finish something difficult through hard work), bar (a block of metal). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A mint in Australia makes the biggest gold bar in the world. It weighs over 520 kilograms. More than 35 people work for three days to make this special bar. It is pure gold. It is worth over 100 million dollars. People from Guinness World Records watch them make it. Now, it is a new world record. The old record is 300 kilograms in Dubai. Australia wants to show the world that it makes the best gold. Soon, people can go to the mint and see this gold bar with their own eyes. Difficult words: mint (a factory which makes metal money and bars), pure (something which has only one substance in it), worth (the money price of something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Scientists have observed a new behavior in terrestrial hermit crabs globally – they are choosing plastic shells over natural ones for protection. Researchers identified 386 crabs using artificial shells, primarily plastic caps, from images posted online. This behavior was found in 10 out of 16 hermit crab species across the Earth’s tropical coasts. Possible reasons for this shift include sexual signaling, the lightness of artificial shells, odor cues , and camouflage in polluted environments. The impact of this behavior on hermit crab evolution requires further investigation. Plastic is a major marine waste and it influences wildlife negatively. Notably, wildlife photographer Shawn Miller’s images were crucial in highlighting this phenomenon. A campaign advocates for hermit crab conservation , discouraging the removal of natural shells from beaches and emphasizing the global issue of plastic waste, which may be addressed by a UN agreement later this year. Difficult words: cue (a signal), camouflage (using materials, colors, or light to make it difficult to be seen), conservation (protection). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Hermit crabs around the world are doing something new – they are choosing plastic shells instead of natural ones. Scientists found this out by looking at pictures on the internet. A photographer named Shawn Miller took many pictures of these crabs, and he wanted to protect them. He says people shouldn’t take away the shells off beaches. Plastic is a big problem for animals. A 2022 report found that plastic waste could almost triple by 2060. Difficult words: show off (to show something or someone that you are proud or special), protect (to keep something or someone safe). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In 1972, during the Apollo 17 mission, astronauts collected soil and rock samples from the moon. Recently, scientists analyzed zircon crystals within a rock collected by astronaut Harrison Schmitt, shedding light on the moon’s age and formation. Their findings indicate that the moon is approximately 40 million years older than previously believed, forming more than 4.46 billion years ago. This insight helps support the theory that a Mars-sized object, named Theia, collided with Earth during the solar system’s early history. This impact sent molten rock into space, forming a debris disk that eventually coalesced into the moon. Using a method called atom probe tomography, scientists confirmed the age of these ancient zircon crystals. These findings are crucial in understanding the moon’s role in stabilizing Earth’s axis and its impact on our planet’s habitability . The moon’s age and formation also hold significance for future deep-space explorations by space agencies like NASA. Difficult words: shed light (to make something clear or understandable), coalesce (to come together), habitability (the quality of being good enough to live in). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino officially cancelled his controversial plan to sell off parts of major tournaments, including the men’s and women’s World Cups, to private investors. He had offered 40 million dollars to every national football association to get them on board, but the idea caused massive backlash around the world. European football boss UEFA even threatened to boycott the 2030 World Cup, which would have meant famous stars like Jude Bellingham missing out entirely. Other global sports bodies quickly joined the criticism too. Seeing how much trouble it caused, Infantino admitted the project created way too many arguments instead of bringing people together, so he pulled the plug after investors backed out. Experts say this whole mess is a huge embarrassment that leaves Infantino’s position looking pretty weak, as fans and officials insisted that football should stay a game for the people rather than big private money. Difficult words: backlash (a strong, sudden, and negative reaction by a large group of people to a decision or event), boycott (an agreement by people or groups to refuse to buy, use, or take part in something as a protest), pull the plug (to stop or cancel a plan, project, or financial support suddenly). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Difficult words: investor (a person or company which puts money into a business or project), boycott (to stop buying or doing something as a protest), embarrassment (a situation which makes someone look crazy or bad in front of others). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Spain deployed its military to the North African enclave of Ceuta after tens of thousands of migrants crossed the border from Morocco by land and sea. Scenes along the border showed people swimming across, scaling boundary fences, and streaming through open gates, which created an emergency for local authorities. Spain’s Supreme Court recently ruled that arriving migrants cannot be immediately rejected without following specific legal procedures to guarantee their rights, which experts believe encouraged the sudden influx . Nine bodies were recovered near the coast during the crisis. However, Spanish authorities quickly managed to reverse the massive rush. With the military present and security measures restored, most of the more than 50,000 people who had crossed the border have already begun heading back to Morocco voluntarily. They said they were exhausted and had no food, and they realized that staying in the enclave wouldn’t be possible. Difficult words: enclave (a piece of land or territory that belongs to one country but is inside or surrounded by another land), scale (to climb up to the top of a high wall, fence, or mountain), influx (the arrival of a very large number of people, money, or things at the same time). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Spanish forces worked quickly to secure the border and manage the crowd. Soon after arriving, most of the 50,000 migrants decided to turn around and walk back to Morocco. Difficult words: enclave (a piece of land or territory which belongs to one country but is inside another country), emergency (a dangerous situation which needs quick action and help), guarantee (to promise or make sure that something will definitely happen). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Cumbria, an alligator snapping turtle named Fluffy was rescued from Urswick Tarn, near Ulverston. Despite its misleading name, this turtle has a spiky appearance and a fierce bite. Denise Chamberlain, familiar with snapping turtles from her time in Florida, recognized it and organized its rescue. These turtles, native to the US, have powerful jaws capable of cutting through bones. Although not illegal as pets in the UK, they are challenging to care for, leading to possible abandonment . Chamberlain, unable to find help, took matters into her own hands, safely capturing Fluffy. The turtle was later examined by Dr. Kate Hornby, who noted its rarity in the UK. Fluffy will be relocated to a specialized reptile center. It’s believed Fluffy was once a pet, underscoring the importance of proper research and care for exotic animals. Difficult words: abandonment (leaving someone or something forever), reptile (a type of animal, such as a snake, turtle, or crocodile), underscore (to emphasize). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The golden ratio is a special number that appears in many places, like nature, art, and buildings. It comes from a number sequence introduced to Europe by Leonardo Fibonacci in 1202, though it was discovered earlier by the Hindu scholar Pingala. This sequence leads to a ratio that creates the “golden rectangle,” a shape that some people believe looks perfect. In the 1860s, Gustav Fechner claimed people preferred this shape, which helped create the idea that the golden ratio represents beauty. However, his study was later disproved . More recent experiments show that most people can’t even recognize the golden rectangle by sight. The golden ratio appears in sunflower spirals and other natural patterns, but nature doesn’t always follow it. Shells, for example, grow based on calcium levels, not math. Some think human faces that match the golden ratio are more beautiful; however, this idea is not supported by science. It can create false beauty standards and misuse real mathematics. The golden ratio is interesting in art and nature, but it is not a rule for beauty. It is only one way to look at the world. Everyone’s view of beauty is different. Difficult words: ratio (a comparison between two numbers or sizes), disproved (shown to be wrong), standard (an idea of what is normal or best). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Some people think this shape looks very nice. Gustav Fechner said people liked it best, but later, others showed that he was not right. The golden ratio is in some flowers and other things in nature, but it is not in everything. For example, snail shells don’t grow with this number. Some people use the golden ratio to say who is beautiful. They use it in apps or pictures on social media. But this is not true. Scientists say the golden ratio cannot show who is or is not beautiful. Everyone is different, and that is okay. Difficult words: sequence (the order in which things follow each other), rectangle (a shape with four sides and four corners), shell (the hard outer part of some animals, for example snails or crabs). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Thousands of firefighters across France and Spain are battling massive wildfires that have forced nearly 375,000 people to evacuate their homes. It is one of Europe’s largest evacuation efforts since World War II. In southwestern France, blazes near Bordeaux have burned tens of thousands of hectares, destroyed property and left thick ash in the air. Meanwhile, thousands have been evacuated in Spain’s Valencia region. Supported by international aircraft and personnel, emergency crews worked around the clock during a brief period of cooler weather to contain the flames. However, many fires remain out of control, and forecasted heatwaves with temperatures up to 38°C threaten to intensify the crisis. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez blamed global warming for escalating disasters and called for national action to address climate emergencies. The damage is terrible, and politicians are already arguing, but local teams and helpful volunteers have managed to keep people safe so far. Difficult words: around the clock (all day and all night without stopping), contain (to stop something dangerous or harmful from spreading or getting worse), intensify (to become stronger, greater, or more serious). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Luckily, no civilians died, but many families cannot return home yet and must stay in emergency shelters . Difficult words: huge (very big or large), civilian (an ordinary person who doesn’t belong to police, army, or firefighting service), shelter (a safe place). Around 600,000 male mosquitoes are being released across the Washington D.C. area this summer to fight rising mosquito populations. Although releasing more insects seems counterintuitive , these male mosquitoes don’t bite humans because only females feed on blood to produce eggs. The released males carry a bacterium called Wolbachia. When these infected males mate with local females, the incompatible bacterial strains stop the eggs from hatching, which makes the females infertile for life. As climate change creates warmer conditions, mosquitoes and the dangerous diseases they carry are expanding into new regions. Experts say that this method is completely safe for humans and local ecosystems, as the bacteria cannot infect people or predators like birds and fish. By continuously releasing these non-biting males over a few weeks, local communities hope to significantly reduce mosquito populations and stop the spread of viruses. Difficult words: counterintuitive (happening in a way that is opposite to what you would naturally expect), mate (to join together to produce young or eggs), incompatible (not able to work, exist, or combine successfully together), infertile (unable to produce young, eggs, or babies). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

It doesn’t harm nature or other animals. Within a few weeks, this project can quickly reduce the mosquito population and help people enjoy being outside in the summer. Difficult words: release (to let a person, animal, or thing go free into an area), mate (to join together to produce young or eggs), hatch (to break out of an egg or give birth to babies). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
